newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to face leaders of hostile parliament.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to face leaders of hostile parliament.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin meets the speakers and party chiefs of both houses of the Russian parliament on Monday, notably to explain last week's accord with NATO, which was savagely criticised by the communist opposition.

The meeting may also touch on two other conflicts between the administration and the legislature -- drastic government budget cuts and the return of art works seized from Germany in World War Two -- as well as this week's planned signing of a union treaty with neighbouring Belarus.

The Kremlin said the meeting, which begins at 1.30 p.m. (0930 GMT), would follow talks on the economy between Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and the two first deputy premiers, Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov.

The president said in a rare television interview last week that he would brief parliamentarians on the deal struck with NATO last week which will allow Moscow and its former Cold War adversary to sign a treaty in Paris on May 27.

Yeltsin characterised the pact as a triumph for Russian diplomacy in the face of a decidedly unwelcome but unstoppable determination on the part of the alliance to extend membership to some of Moscow's old Warsaw Pact allies in eastern Europe.

He said Moscow had won the key security concessions it had sought -- notably binding assurances from the West not to push its nuclear and other military hardware closer to Russia's borders and a decisive say for Russia in NATO decisions.
Such talk is part of a delicate balancing act. Both parties are anxious to sell the deal to their allies and domestic constituents while emphasising the accord will actually stick.

Western leaders, keen to avoid offending potential new NATO members like Poland, have played down any suggestion the Kremlin would have a veto over all the alliance's affairs. Moscow admitted its blocking vote only covers decisions affecting it.
Russian communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said the treaty betrayed the Soviet Union's millions of war dead. "This treaty is practically an act of capitulation," he said at the weekend.

In what may partly have been a bid to deflect that sort of criticism at home, where Zyuganov's party dominates the State Duma lower house of parliament, Yeltsin invited French President Jacques Chirac for a flying visit on Sunday.
Chirac, stopping off on his return from a trip to China, duly obliged by describing the NATO-Russia pact as "a great victory for Russia" and "a personal victory for President Yeltsin".

The treaty does not need ratification by the Russian parliament. That is fortunate for Yeltsin since even the once docile Federation Council upper house turned against him last week, supporting a Duma move to overturn the presidential veto on a bill to block Yeltsin's promise to return German treasures.
Yeltsin is expected to send the bill to the Constitutional Court this week, insisting it breaks international law.

More pressingly, Yeltsin may want to try to broker a compromise between parliament and the government over ministers' plans to slash 1997 budget spending by a fifth because of a huge shortfall in tax revenue in the first quarter.
Chernomyrdin, indicating a possible compromise with the communists, said he might cut spending by less than forecast.
Yeltsin is due to sign an expanded document completing a union with Belarus on Friday. But the scheme seems to have run into trouble in recent days.
Conservative Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko, long a champion of reuniting the former Soviet states, has criticised Moscow's bid to dominate the union.
